solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Complete unfinished narrow band on a silk scarf

indicators.note: something unfinished stops short, so the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: to do a job is to complete it
a patte is a narrow band holding a belt in place, here without its last letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone finishing off a half-made trim on a silk scarf.
explanation.walkthrough: A patte is a Chambers word for a narrow strap or band, and it loses its tail. In an across clue, 'on' simply puts the band ahead of the final A.
explanation.definitionFit: A dopatta (or dupatta) is the long light scarf of silk or muslin worn in South Asia, so it is a direct dictionary synonym.

clue.text: Tab something round sashes on ankle

blocks.note: a disc is any flat round thing
an obi is the broad sash worn with a kimono
cuit is a Scots word for the ankle

explanation.surface: Describing a decorative tab, something round with sashes worn at the ankle.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces run across the word break: DISC + OBIS + CUIT reads as DISCO BISCUIT. 'Tab' looks like a label or loop of fabric, but it is slang for a pill.
explanation.definitionFit: Disco biscuit is club slang for an ecstasy tablet, and tab is the shortened word for such a pill, so both name the same drug dose.

clue.text: Old ropes with loose ends make out to be twisted

indicators.note: ends that come loose fall off, so each word drops its final letter
twisting something bends it from its original shape, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
the word without its last letter

explanation.surface: Frayed old ropes with loose ends that look as though they have been twisted.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words of 'make out' lose their tail letters, leaving MAK and OU, which rearrange into OAKUM. 'Old ropes with loose ends' reads like one long definition, but only 'Old ropes' is.
explanation.definitionFit: Oakum is loose fibre got by untwisting and picking apart old hemp ropes, used for caulking ships' seams.

clue.text: Once declared amateur’s separate in fighting

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for amateur
to redd is a Scots and dialect verb for parting combatants in a fight

explanation.surface: An amateur boxer stepping in to pull apart two fighters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' flags an archaic word: AREDD is a Spenserian form found in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: Aread or aredd is an obsolete verb meaning to declare or explain, and its past form serves for declared in older English.

clue.text: Surgical instrument for cutting back of neck right back

indicators.note: going back means heading the other way, so the letters run in the opposite order

blocks.note: the nape is the back of the neck
RT is a standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A surgeon's tool for cutting at the back of the neck, applied right at the back.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'back' belongs to the phrase for the neck; only the final 'back' is the signal to turn everything around. RT is the abbreviation for right.
explanation.definitionFit: A trepan is a cylindrical saw surgeons use to remove a disc of bone from the skull, a precise synonym for that cutting tool.

clue.text: Nearly alarm carrying uranium containing gold …

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the word stops one letter short
to carry something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: to arouse is to alarm or stir up; the last letter is dropped
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: A warning that some ore holds both uranium and gold, trailing into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The dots join this clue to 7 down, which also turns on gold. The U goes in right after the opening A.
explanation.definitionFit: Aurous is the chemistry adjective for compounds of univalent gold, so it describes something with gold in it.

clue.text: Purgative? There’s spattering around indeed!

indicators.note: to be around something is to surround it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: jap is a Scots word meaning to splash or spatter
la is an old exclamation meaning lo or indeed

explanation.surface: A wry remark that a laxative has left mess splashed everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are Scots or archaic words from Chambers: one means to splash, the other is an old exclamation. The exclamation mark suits 'indeed' as an interjection.
explanation.definitionFit: Jalap is the dried root of a Mexican plant, long used in medicine as a strong laxative.

clue.text: … gold part bearing hint of extraordinary halo

indicators.note: a hint is the smallest trace, so only the opening letter is kept
to bear is to carry, so one piece is carried inside another

blocks.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold
an actor's part is a role
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Continuing 5 down: a gold piece carrying a remarkable halo.
explanation.walkthrough: The leading dots pick up gold from 5 down. The E goes in after the R of ROLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An aureole is the radiance of light circling the head or body of a holy figure in art, the same thing as a halo.

clue.text: Fine linen female’s covered in custard

indicators.note: what is covered in a word is part of it; reading it off leaves the rest of that word as the answer

blocks.note: a flawn is an old word for a custard or flan
F is the abbreviation for female

explanation.surface: A woman's fine linen gets spattered with custard.
explanation.walkthrough: The custard word is the answer with a female F on top, so the answer plus F is covered in it; taking the F away leaves the linen.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawn is a very fine sheer cotton or linen cloth, used for handkerchiefs and bishops' sleeves.

clue.text: Stonemason’s tool breaking rag uncovered mistakes

indicators.note: something breaking falls apart and can be rebuilt in a new order
with its covering stripped, a word loses its outside letters at each end

blocks.note: taken as written
gaffes are blunders, here without their first and last letters

explanation.surface: A stonemason's tool smashing through a cloth, the mistakes laid bare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mistakes' gives GAFFES, which is stripped to AFFE; that joins RAG as the letters to break up.
explanation.definitionFit: An agraffe is a cramp-iron that masons and builders use to hold blocks of stone together, a technical tool sense.

clue.text: Temper most of raging behaviour turning to stone

indicators.note: most of a thing is all but a little, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: a pet is a fit of sulky temper
rife means raging or widespread, as a disease is
action is conduct or behaviour

explanation.surface: A moody person's raging behaviour that ends in stony silence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Temper' looks like a verb meaning to moderate, but it is the noun: to be in a pet is to be in a sulk.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrifaction is the process of organic matter becoming stone, so the noun phrase for that process is an exact equivalent.

clue.text: Spring clean after cottage cleared out guest room

indicators.note: clearing out empties the inside, so only the two outer letters stay
to spring is to leap about, so the letters jump into a new order
coming after puts one piece behind the other in the answer

blocks.note: the first and last letters of the word
taken as written

explanation.surface: Doing the spring clean once the holiday cottage has been emptied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring clean' reads as one household chore, but 'Spring' is the instruction acting on 'clean'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cenacle is an upper room for dining, especially the one of the Last Supper, so a room for guests fits.

clue.text: Rightly stalling question about good art forgery

indicators.note: to stall something is to shut it up in a stall, so one piece is penned inside another

blocks.note: true can mean rightly, as in aiming true
QU is the abbreviation for question
A is an abbreviation for about, approximately
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A dealer rightly holding back a question over whether a work is a fake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stalling' suggests delay, but here it means housing in a stall: the three short pieces sit inside the word for rightly.
explanation.definitionFit: Truquage is a French-derived term for faking works of art, so it names the forging of art directly.

clue.text: Doubling endeavours checking territory for mozzies

indicators.note: doubling back means turning round on your path, so the letters run the other way
to check is to hold back or restrain, so one piece holds another inside

blocks.note: to seek to do something is to endeavour
Ter. is an abbreviation for territory

explanation.surface: Twice the effort spent checking an area for mosquitoes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doubling' suggests repetition, but it means doubling back. Mozzies is Australian and British slang for mosquitoes.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeeter is informal North American and Australian slang for a mosquito, matching the colloquial plural mozzies.

clue.text: Maybe crack’s a little unsafe for a covered drain

indicators.note: read as 'has', so the word has one of its letters exchanged for a new one
a little of a word is just a scrap of it, its opening letter

blocks.note: candy is street slang for drugs, of which crack is one example
the letter to be swapped out
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A crack in the cover of a drain makes it a little unsafe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crack' looks like a fissure in the drain, but it is the drug, and 'Maybe' marks it as one example of drugs in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Cundy is a Scots and dialect word, listed in Chambers, for a covered drain or a culvert.

clue.text: Debar’s name for bit of bread?

indicators.note: one thing standing for another means it takes its place

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: Asking what a word means for a scrap of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter replaced is B, the first letter of 'bread', so 'bit of bread' also points to it. Bread is slang for money, which the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: The denar is the currency unit of North Macedonia, so it is a piece of money, and bread is slang for cash.

clue.text: Daffy Duck’s leading tailed frequent fool?

indicators.note: to lead is to go in front, so this piece comes first
to tail fruit is to cut off its end, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O
daffy means crazy
to haunt a place is to frequent it; its last letter is cut

explanation.surface: Daffy Duck, the cartoon character, playing the regular clown.
explanation.walkthrough: The cartoon name splits into two pieces, with the duck put in front of the daffiness. In cricket a duck is a batsman's score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: Omadhaun is an Irish word, from Gaelic, for a foolish or simple person, so it is a regional synonym.

clue.text: Scare at waste plant

indicators.note: to lay waste is to wreck, so the letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fright at a rubbish dump.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Waste' looks like a noun for rubbish, but it is a verb telling you to wreck the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Cat's-ear is a dandelion-like wild flower with hairy leaves, a named species of plant.

clue.text: Muscle protein not quite having effect

indicators.note: not quite all of it means stopping just short, so the final letter goes

blocks.note: acting means having an effect, as a drug is said to act; its last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A muscle protein supplement that is not quite working.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the protein barely works; 'not quite' acts only on the phrase after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Actin is one of the two main proteins, with myosin, whose filaments slide together to make muscle contract.

clue.text: Kind of sweet performing carol with Hawaiian?

indicators.note: performing a piece means working it into a new rendition, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
a Hawaiian is a kind of pizza, and za is slang for pizza; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: Sweet carol singing with a Hawaiian performer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hawaiian' looks like a person singing along, but it is the ham-and-pineapple pizza.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcorza is a Spanish sugar paste or icing used for sweetmeats, so it names a particular confection.

clue.text: Nozzles carrying blasts of air yet sure to get hot

indicators.note: things that get hot become agitated and excited, so the letters are stirred up

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Furnace nozzles that blow air, certain to grow hot.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition runs long, so 'blasts of air' seems to belong to the wordplay; it does not.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuyeres are the pipes through which air is blown into a blast furnace or forge, so they are air-blast nozzles.

clue.text: Food includes large buffet

indicators.note: to include something is to take it in, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: scaff is a Scots word for food
L is the abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: A buffet meal that offers plenty of food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Buffet' reads as a spread of food, but it is the verb meaning to strike; the food word is Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: To sclaff is to strike or buffet, especially to hit the ground behind a golf ball, a Scots verb of striking.

clue.text: Planted in soil lupin’s a large plant

indicators.note: something planted in the ground sits buried within it, so the answer lies inside the following words

blocks.note: letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A gardener remarks that the lupin in their bed has grown huge.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer starts inside the word for earth and ends one letter short of the end of the flower name.
explanation.definitionFit: The illupi, or mahwa, is a large Indian tree whose seeds give an oil, so it is a big plant.

clue.text: Transparent gem extracted from variolites

indicators.note: what is extracted is drawn out of something, so the answer is taken from within a word

blocks.note: letters three to eight of the word

explanation.surface: A clear gemstone mined from variolite rock.
explanation.walkthrough: Variolite is a real rock, so the surface reads as geology; the gem sits inside its plural.
explanation.definitionFit: Iolite is a transparent violet-blue gem form of the mineral cordierite, cut as a precious stone.

clue.text: Freeman’s not at UK’s national gallery

indicators.note: not having something means it is missing, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: taken as written
the Tate is Britain's national gallery of British and modern art

explanation.surface: A Freeman of the city is not to be found at the national gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: The Tate is the national collection of British and modern art, with galleries in London and elsewhere. 'Freeman' suggests the civic honour, but here it is ancient Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Athens a thete was a free citizen of the lowest property class, a freeman who was not a slave.

clue.text: Shocking time round Havana?

indicators.note: to turn round is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
a Havana is a Cuban cigar; the question mark flags it as an example

explanation.surface: A dreadful spell spent travelling around the Cuban capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Havana' looks like the city, but it is a cigar named after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tragic and shocking are both adjectives for an event that is dreadful and deeply distressing, so they are near synonyms.

clue.text: Reduced fines or compliance due to lord’s superior

indicators.note: something reduced to rubble is broken down, so the letters are smashed and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written
the word cut down to its opening letter, 'Reduced' acting on it too

explanation.surface: A feudal tenant's lowered fines or obedience owed to the lord above his own lord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reduced' works twice: it shortens the last word to one letter and breaks up the whole collection.
explanation.definitionFit: Forinsec is a feudal term for service owed not to one's immediate lord but to the lord above him.

clue.text: Face plant right in snow

indicators.note: to plant something is to set it down into a place
in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
névé is granular snow at the head of a glacier

explanation.surface: A skier falling face first into the snow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Face plant' reads as a skiing fall, but 'Face' is the definition and 'plant' starts the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To nerve yourself is to steel yourself, and to face something is to confront it with courage, a verb sense.

clue.text: Quench unbounded enthusiasm

indicators.note: with no bounds a word has no edges, so its first and last letters go

blocks.note: to destroy can mean to quench or extinguish; both ends of that word are removed

explanation.surface: Putting out boundless zeal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unbounded enthusiasm' looks like one phrase, but 'unbounded' acts on the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Estro is an Italian loan word for poetic fervour or creative enthusiasm, kept in Chambers.

clue.text: Established principles without manuscript volume

blocks.note: a code is a settled set of rules or principles
x is short for ex, Latin for without, as in xd for ex dividend

explanation.surface: Established rules that have no written book behind them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like an instruction to remove something, but it supplies a letter: ex means without, abbreviated to x in finance.
explanation.definitionFit: A codex is an ancient manuscript in book form rather than a scroll, so it is a handwritten volume.

clue.text: Share half of pods for tanning and dyeing

indicators.note: half of something is what remains when the other half goes

blocks.note: these pods come from a tropical American tree whose doubled name is two identical halves

explanation.surface: Splitting a crop of pods meant for the leather and dye trades.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant name is a doubled word, so either half gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A divi is informal British for a dividend, a person's portion or share of the profits.

clue.text: Spider perhaps holding end of cue in baulk

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that is kept
to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: in snooker a spider is a type of rest for the cue
the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A snooker player using the spider to cue from the baulk area of the table.
explanation.walkthrough: In snooker the spider is a rest with a raised head, and baulk is an area of the table, but here 'baulk' is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Reest is a Scots verb for a horse refusing to move, the same as to baulk or jib.

clue.text: Understand age computing’s brought about? That’s us

indicators.note: to bring a boat about is to turn it, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: to dig is slang for to understand
an era is an age
IT is information technology, that is computing

explanation.surface: Proud tech experts congratulating themselves on what the computer age has achieved.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a cheeky claim by the setter that crossword solvers working online are the computer-savvy elite.
explanation.definitionFit: Digerati are people expert in digital technology, and the setter playfully counts solvers among that group.

clue.text: One-zero match’s covered in Russian news

indicators.note: what is covered in something is wrapped inside it

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one and Z stands for zero, as in the letter used for a nought
a vesta is a short friction match
the numeral again, supplied a second time by the same word

explanation.surface: A one-nil football result reported in the Russian papers.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening pair is I and Z, but a second I is needed inside the match word, and only 'One' can supply it, so it seems to work twice; treat this parse as uncertain.
explanation.definitionFit: Izvestia is a leading Russian daily newspaper whose title is the Russian word for news.

clue.text: Apparition? Charlie perhaps picking up electric current

indicators.note: to pick something up is to take it on board, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a tash is a moustache, and a Charlie Chaplin is one style of it
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A ghost sighting: perhaps it was Charlie, crackling with electricity.
explanation.walkthrough: Tash is British slang for a moustache, and Charlie Chaplin's toothbrush style is the example the question of 'perhaps' implies.
explanation.definitionFit: Taish is a Scots Highland word for a vision or apparition, especially a wraith seen as an omen of death.

clue.text: Augment limit to personnel applied to level in organisation

indicators.note: a limit is the boundary at the far edge, so only the closing letter is kept

blocks.note: eche is a Shakespearean form of eke, to augment
the last letter of the word
on means placed against or applied to

explanation.surface: Raising the cap on staff numbers as it applies to each level of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Limit to personnel' sounds like a headcount cap, but it only asks for the closing letter. Eche is an archaic word Shakespeare uses.
explanation.definitionFit: An echelon is a rank or grade in a hierarchy, so it is one level of an organisation.
